titleStmt.title: Interview with Charles Jordan, Jr., May 30, 2003
titleStmt.author: Thomas Swope

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Charles Jordan, Jr. was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: '41. I was living in Ferris (ph) County at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were obviously in high school?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: I actually rather graduated in the early part of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Do you have distinct memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes and no. I mean, my folks were away and I happened to be listening to the radio and I heard it on the radio. And I didn't really know what it was all about at that time. And of course, communications then were only radio and that's all you had to listen to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember -- let's see. You graduated in '44. Do you remember doing anything in school for the war effort during the first couple of years of the war?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: No. I actually went from school -- high school to basic training. But, they give me my diploma because I was to graduate in the Spring and I went in the -- the first part of the year I went into the service. I took basic training at Camp Lynn in Florida and at that time, I thought I was going to the Pacific because we were in all swampy land of Florida. And after basic training, why, I had a two-week leave and then, went overseas to England. And I think it took us five or six days to go over there. We went over there by ourselves, no convoy. And I think there were 15,000 troops on the boat. And of course, I was seasick all the way over. And we landed in England, and why, I was a little bit wobbly on my legs because of being seasick. It just felt like the island was tilting too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you land in England?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Where at?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: When? I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Approximately. Was it sometime in December of '44 or --

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: It was the Summer of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: It was in May or something like that, because at that time, we only had six weeks of basic training and they were looking for more volunteers so I was one of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: I was in England there for awhile and on the coast a short while. But, then, we left when everybody else did, and I was a replacement then. I went across in Canadian-operated landing craft. I forget but I think they called it LCI or something like that. Then, we unloaded from that onto landing barges on Omaha Beach. And of course, Omaha Beach was already taken, but there was still a lot of demonstration on the beach. And then we just moved up to our place before we were deployed to a division. And I ended up in the 83rd Division on Omaha Beach or on the Normandy area there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that still in June of '44 when you landed over there?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. And my observation of the beach was really devastated, but, I feel that we could have done a better job of going in on that beach because a lot of the installations were intact which allowed the Germans to do a little harder fighting and had a lot of places to hide. So, that was -- I felt was one of our shortcomings there. They should have sent more aircraft in and more artillery and boats further on the beach instead of right directly on the beach. Because they were on the top of the hill. So, but, I don't quite understand why the Germans were able to build all of these facilities on the beach that we didn't see what was going on. All of these obstacles underwater and building pill boxes and trenches and so forth that we couldn't have seen that and destroyed them while they was under construction. Well, then, I was assigned to the 83rd Division. And at that time, we were going to St. Lo. And I remember the airplanes that were going to do the bombing of St. Lo, they had about I imagine, over three thousand planes that flew across there during the day to blow up the city. But, it seems like the Germans came off out of the rubble and were there anyway, which caused a lot of fierce fighting and we were in hedgerow country.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You remember that day?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was -- we knew the basic things, but they were still by the book. We did everything just alike. It seemed like the Germans had everything "zeroed in" on the hedgerows. Every roadway seemed to be artillery covered. And then, it was difficult for our tanks to maneuver because they were on top of those hedgerows and they got knocked off right away. And our tanks weren't built to withstand those 88's. And they could use them horizontal firing as well as aircraft firing. And the armored wasn't as heavy as the Germans' tanks. And they resisted again. I thought when I first went in these hedgerows, I thought a hedgerow was noting but brush. Well, I found out that they consist of a lot of piled-up dirt, which is maybe six or seven feet high. And every field was just like a checkerboard with an opening to get in and out of the fields. So, you either had to work your way around and seize the mines and everything that were everyplace, and it just seemed like every time you moved, they knew where you was at. But, I can say one thing about the American soldier is that I'd never seen a person or persons that were so outstanding in what they had to do. I mean, they didn't have to be told by officers because some of our officers weren't that good. But, the basic, the GI, took it upon himself to take an obstacle however he could. And that's the way we went all the way through. On the coast, we went up to the Kirtney (ph) Peninsula. I'd seen behind the Germans on the coast there, so, they couldn't turn their guns around because it was all faced out towards the ocean or the channel. But, it was one devastation of junkyard you might say, just equipment everyplace, ammunition. I'd seen a train that had been blown up, ammunition scattered everywhere. Then, we worked up toward Cherbourg on the coast and we came to this town, resort town of, I think it was Dennard on the coast. Then, we cleared that area out, and then, there was an island off there that there was a German garrison on that they brought out the big guns and fired pointblank on this island and then, they dive bombed the planes, and give it -- I volunteered to go out on that mission, but, it seemed like that the Germans gave up. So, the General, he went out to take their surrender. But, there was a lot of free French around there, and I seen they brought these girls that collaborated with the Germans, they brought them down to the center of town and cut all their hair off, right in the center. And then, there was a lot of dead horses and stuff laying around. And it wasn't too good of a site. So, we moved up along the peninsula there where the Germans had their U-boats and we bottled them off. And I guess they had them there the rest of the war and kept them bottled up there. But, we ran a lot of patrols back in there. And we were taking casualties every day on patrols and found out that they were directly under our nose a lot of the times. The worse time that I think that all of us hated was nightfall and early morning because you don't know where the Germans were; they ran patrols and they could be in with you or we could be in with them and you didn't know whether they were going to attack or what was going to come off. It was -- you really had to look out for everything. And when you're 18 years old, why you grow up pretty fast. Then, we was on the drive when Patton made the breakthrough, and we got beyond and extended our supply lines. We didn't have any food and we had to scrounge around the French villages to find food to eat until our supplies caught up with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were the French people nice to you at that point?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. We never seen any French people in the towns there. They all evacuated the towns. But, as soon as the town was taken, they were all coming back in on the roads, which were cut up pretty bad. But, the first thing they seemed to open up was the bake shop, and we got bread because none of those stores that I ever seen didn't have a stick of food in them. And of course, when they come back in some of these towns, they didn't have a place to stay either. But usually they was on a two-wheel cart pulled by a horse or pulled by people, and we had to live day-by-day. And there was as far as taking a bath, why you had to take it wherever you could, whether it be in a watering trough or out of a helmet. The first shower I had was in Luxembourg. That was in a beer refinery or company. And I had the first taste of beer there. But, Luxembourg was the first, actually I thought, modern city that wasn't destroyed and that we had stayed right in Luxembourg and one of my first leaves was to go uptown. But, there were still snipers in it, so, we had to watch pretty carefully. And went to this one hotel expecting to get something decent to eat. And all they had was our tin rations they served. And after that, we moved out of Luxembourg and our job was to move the Germans across the Moselle River. And there several of these towns along the Moselle that we cleaned out. And that was where I was on the first patrol of our division to cross the Moselle one night into Germany. And we had some pretty fierce fighting along those towns until we got them cleared out. And then, we moved. From there, we went up into Belgium through Metz. And while in Metz, we stayed in a French barracks up there on the Maginal (ph) line. And the Germans had shuttered it every night at chow time. And then, we had the opportunity, our company, to go down on the Maginal Line which was very interesting. But, I'd say it was very stupid for the French to build something like that because it was underground and we went down underground and we didn't have -- there was no electric down there, but we got lights and went down in there. And they had one main phone, and off this tunnel, they had barracks, hospitals and so forth, and they had these guns that were on hydraulic lifts and on top of the ground, that had this -- there was a steel dome on it. Then, the guys sat down in the chair down below and with a periscope looked out the domes to fire guns, but, I don't think they ever used that line, because where they had doors, the went different areas, they had moots in front of these doors. But, everything was pointing one way. Then, if the Germans come direct, they might have encountered something, but they went around it. I mean, they didn't even phase it. I mean, the guys were more in danger being in it than they were out of it. It was something. I just couldn't believe it. Even today, I couldn't understand why they did something like this. And then, we practiced -- we used the Moselle Line to practice pillbox attacks on the Siegfried Line. And we -- after that, we moved into Belgium. We went into Liege and Saint Vith. We were on our way up into Herkin Forest. And that was to me, a real worst time I ever seen because of the shell bursts and the trees, the trees blowing down. The Germans being entrenched, and there was this -- you just had to force them out. And the artillery was fierce in that area. Aukin (ph) was completely destroyed. Then, we pushed out in another forest during. I think it was on our left. And that was shelled just about night and day. And you could look down into that, and there were fires burning down there all night long. Then, we pushed down --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the name of the town again where the fires were burning?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: During.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: I think it was 100,000 population, the town was. But, then we pushed down into a town of Gaye, which was right as you left the Herkin Forest which was on the way to the Collum Plains. And we spent -- we attacked at Gaye. We took that with a lot of guys. And tanks were getting hit. We finally got the new tanks up there which were the bigger tanks, the heavy tanks, with the 90 millimeter on them. But, our tanks would just take a hit and the bullet would go right through it, right through the front of it or side, and the first thing they would do -- most of all, our tanks would burn up, just blow up, because the way they were built. And most of the people, all of the guys, tied sandbags on the outside, whatever they could to keep from letting that shell go through. And then, we -- it's at night you had to set up your own booby traps because when you are around an outpost, you had to have some protection from them crawling up to you. So, would just take hand grenades and sometimes we would take the C-ration cans and go to those hedgerows and we dug a trip wire and we took and put the hand grenade in the C-ration can and dug it out in the field there and put a trip wire across over the hedgerow so anybody that would come up on the hedgerow or something, why, they trip that wire and pull the pin on the grenade and you knew somebody was there. And you know, you just had to stay -- in the forest you had to stay -- every time a shell come in close, why you were just out closer to on top of the hole. And when we first moved in Herkin Forest, why, a buddy of mine, we had picked out an area that the Germans had dug and so, the Captain said, "I want you to take some people and go out there and build a new outpost out in front." And we dug all night, and you could hear the shrapnel hitting the side of the hole as you are digging. And the two guys that took -- that he originally picked, they were both dead in the morning, concussion, a shell hit near the hole. So, I had narrow escapes. I laid down on a mine, it happened to be a tank mine up in a hedgerow, and I came back after going down and somebody had gone down on a mine and so they had my stuff torn off one spot, and had some sticks stuck in the ground and tape around it and here I had laid on that mine all night.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know it when you were laying there?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: No. It was just clean ground. Of course, we knew that night.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And then, down there near Metz, we were going to attack a division wise, and we were going to attack Chrysler Moselle. And you can't imagine moving a whole division at night in trucks and getting off and walking the rest of the way to get in place for an attack across the Moselle. Fortunately, for some unknown reason, it was called off. So we missed out on that Moselle crossing, because on patrols across there, you would get up along the roads and Germans were moving. Most everything there moving was the forces, you know, and carts. So, we took our share of prisoners and back in Normandy I took an SS troop officer. And he didn't like it too well. But, these are things that you encountered everyday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did he try to do, anything?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: He just give me a dirty look. When I took his pistol away from him, why he was about ready to go after me, but he didn't have a chance. And we had a lot of things that happened, oh, then, after -- that's when the breakthrough came. And then, we went back up into Belgium, a place called St. Myth, they called it the "bloody five corners." And that's where our outfit was deployed, in there, and I was just there a few days and I got hit. And --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you get hit?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: With a mortar. And at the same time, I had my feet froze. And we were very poorly equipped for American fighting. We had our heavy wool coats, but when that got wet, that was a slight wearing of a suit of armor, I mean, it was so heavy. Our feet, we didn't have shoe packs; we just had our regular shoes. And then, we did get some goulaches, I call them. But, we couldn't wear them when we were attacking because it was just too cumbersome to run with them. And we saw -- there was just mud, snow and cold. That's all there was. I mean, you had to stand in holes. You didn't have a chance. If you got out of them, you had to get moving. And I just -- it's just tattooed in my mind; I can't... (Delay) (Honorable gentleman was crying) I just can't forget. (Delay again) So I was evacuated back to the chain of hospitals in Paris. And they put me on a hospital boat back to England. And I think it was those hospital ships were so just beautiful inside. I mean, they were just pure white. And after in England for awhile, they sent me back to the United States, and I landed in New York, and they asked me where the closest hospital I knew was, and I told them Triump, which was in Cleveland there. So I ended up down in San Antone, Texas, Fort Sam Houston Hospital until I was discharged.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were your wounds?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, back and face. And of course, I had my feet froze, which I still have trouble today with them. But, as they say, they just didn't have the equipment to do this stuff, I mean. And it just seemed like they didn't think about it or they didn't think things would happen. We just -- a whole lot of things we could have that we didn't have, and I say I think it was our -- the guys at issue that won this war. But, there is a lot more things happened that I -- everyday something happens. I mean, it was just you have guys with you one day and the next day, they are not there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: That's the way it went every day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You had close guys?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes, real close.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Now the 83rd has a yearly reunion every year that I've been going to and I ran across some of my buddies which were Company

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: 331st, and we get together once a year in various locations to just reminisce.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: (Totally inaudible question)

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: It was after Christmas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: After Christmas?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. See, Saint Vith in Bastonne, we went to Bastonne when we got in Germany. Bastonne wasn't even touched. It was still standing. But, I can't say that afterwards. But, I think Patton had the right idea. He had a hard breakthrough and leave the pockets. But, I had been following the history of World War II, and I could see where we could have done a lot better tactic wise. That breakthrough should never have happened if we had been on our feet and listened to people that said what was coming. We took it -- we thought we had them beat, but, we didn't. And then, they put a green division up there where they came and they didn't have a chance. They had no idea what was coming because they couldn't fight against those German tanks, and the blitzkrieg they put on, you know. And unfortunately the weather was against us in that area. I think that's the most snow that they had in that area.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In that area in many years (inaudible far from microphone)

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And the British wanted to hole up for the winter, and they started building cabins like to house themselves in and we never knew what a cabin was or we was lucky to find a half blown-down house. There are these memories now popping back at me. In Luxembourg there, we resisted in this town on the Moselle there that a friend of mine caught this chicken and we were going to cook it up, you know. And we were in this house and we got the chicken and we got it cleaned and started the fire in the stove and the first think, you know, the Germans shelled up and blew the roof off of the house. So, we didn't get any chicken.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't get it cooked?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. Well, but, our clothing and everything, we expected gas from the Germans. We had all this impregnated clothes, and wore arm bands and everything like that and had our gas masks. But, fortunately, this guy, being as stupid as he was, Hitler, he didn't use it. We were real fortunate, because after awhile we didn't carry those gas masks with us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were these arm bands colored or something like that?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. These impregnated clothes were our fatigues, which were just -- they were heavy. They were stiff like they had starch in them. And that's the only protection that we had.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: It was just unbelievable what guys went through. I just wished that we had some of the stuff that they have today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: We would have shortened that place up real quick like.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long were you in the hospital at Sam Houston?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: I think I was there a couple of months. But, that was probably my best time in the Army. Fort Sam Houston there is beautiful, the hospital area. I mean, it had everything there you wanted, you know. They had good food, they had good accommodations, you know. It just wasn't -- the hospital, you know, just wasn't like living in a barracks, and it was nice. They had shows and stuff.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of shows did you go to?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, they had dances and things like that, and they would take a group of people out on picnics, the ones that could, to some of the ranches. San Antone, downtown, was always a place where there was a lot of Air Corps guys there. And this river runs through San Antone. And the infantry guys were trying to throw the air force into the water. But, we had -- the German prisoners in this country, I mean, had it made. I mean, they had the best of everything. I mean, they had very little guards on them. The first ones I seen was in Florida, in Camp Blaney (ph) down there. They were taken from Africa. But, they would try to make fun of some of the guys down there on bayonet practice. One day a group of us took off after them. And they didn't bother us any more.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why were they so close to bayonet practice; what were they doing there?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Cleaning up the grounds, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Maintenance?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Maintenance work, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: There were guys with bayonets?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. These guys had a free run, you might say. They may have two or three guards with them, but, they had everything that we had. Except for -- I mean, I ran across a place over there in Pennsylvania at the CC camps built. They had German prisoners there during the war. Because there was one German prisoner brought his family back to show them where he stayed. But, there wasn't a fence around that place. They would take these German prisoners in town at night and the weekends and pick them up and bring them back at camp. But, they did a lot of good there; they built -- they planted trees; they did a lot of work. But, the German prisoners had it made far better than our guys, because they were put to work and where our guys were in a concentration camp like. And the food was horrible. And I come durn near being captured a few times myself.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah? Tell me about that.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I just fought my way out of it. I mean, just got too far ahead of the company. I lost track of the company, especially these night attacks, you don't know where anybody is. You are out there and you know your company is there, and one night, the whole company pulled out and I didn't know it and there was just me and the Frenchman there holding off these Germans. And the thing that moved me was the grenade that came over and blew my gun in the air and I took off. And that's when I found out there was nobody there. And I ran across the field. I had a real French guy with me for quite a long time. We run across this field and those trenches I swear they was going through our legs and everything. And we ran and I seen another trench down there and I says -- I ducked behind this tree and I looked and I could see in the dark, the moonlight, the little bit that we did and I tried to make those helmets out, you know, the guys down in those trenches and I said, "Boy, what am I going to do with myself?" You know. So, I hollered, I says, if it is German, I'll spray the trench, but, I hollered at the guys and I says, "Coming in, man; coming in; don't shoot." And got to the trench and got in there and had my gun in there and seen this German coming down with his hand in the air and he wanted to give up. And I could only see one hand, and I said, "That's enough out of you, buddy." And when he went down, he had a grenade in his hand. If he had threw that grenade in the trench, there would have been a lot of us not here. But, that's what I hate about night. So, it's such a -- I couldn't go through it again. But, I'm glad I got out of it, but there's a hell of a lot that didn't get out of it. I think there could be more saved if we had done things a little differently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you lead scout a lot of the time?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: No. But, there was this lieutenant always got me to lead patrols.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And it seemed like I was on a patrol every day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And we would go behind the German lines and try to find out what they're doing, you know. And so, there was a touch-and-go situation, I mean. You never knew who was behind the tree. I mean, some of our guys got hit by snipers that were in the trees; we didn't know they were there. You might find them anyplace, you know. You didn't know what you were going to come upon. But, that's the way you lived every day. And as I say, I can't say too much for the GI and I hope they are the same today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: At mail call, did you get much mail or packages from home?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, if you are in a spot, yes. You didn't get it every day because they didn't -- just like food, they didn't bring it out every day; it was too close to the front. It was too dangerous. For them to bring that food out there, you had to live off of rations. But, you did get mail once in awhile. I mean, you was on the line practically every day, you know. And then, when packages did come, why, there was such a mess that everything was crumbs. And if you was a smoker, you could -- they had piles of cigarettes up there that looked like they was dumped out of the dump cart. You could have all you want, but I never smoked, but it was difficult for a lot of guys. I had a patrol that they were so close to the front they would try to smoke, you know, put their head under a blanket. And I told them, I says, "Crack, they can smell that doggone smoke." And so, I tried to curtail that kind of stuff, you know. You didn't dare. Just a little bit of light at night would show up for a long ways, you know. But, it seemed something was kind of weird when we were in Herkin Forest there. It seemed like a Christmas tree was dropped from the air. It just come down and sparkled all the way down. Never could figure it out. Every night there was some German down there in the woods hollering, "Hey, Joe. Hey, Joe. Where are you?" And it was really nerve wracking, you know. And of course, there were a lot of trip flares and stuff that would protect us at night.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But, there were flares being dropped from planes?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Oh, yes. You could see that flare.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: night?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: You could see them down through there. Some of them would come big globs of it, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: From the trees?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, everyplace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Everyplace.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But, it made you feel Christmas, huh!

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, these were like lights at night, you know, because you had those flares go up every once in awhile, you know, to lighten the area up, and you had to not be too out in the open when they went up. You would see the airplanes every day, I mean, flying up there, there was not that big of a vapor trail, then you would see those fighters escorting them, just dots up there amongst them, you know. We always felt pretty good about that. Then, of course, we got pretty close to where they were shooting off the buzz launch and we could see them pretty close where they were throwing up. One night up there in Luxembourg, one went off and the durn thing came right around back at them and hit not too far from where we were. What turned it around, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was while they were shooting at Antwerp or something?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yes. Antwerp or Engel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And they were pretty low and they were just being shot off, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Until they gained altitude they just sound like a motor boat. But, there's all kinds of noises in the war. It's, I don't know --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did your family get a chance to visit you when you were in the hospital?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Too far a trip?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, they could have come down but transportation in them days is either train and the trains were loaded with -- when you are traveling a troop train, why, it was loaded to the gill and you slept and ate right there on the train, you know. And of course, they would pick out a route that they would stop, and when you stopped, why, the USO was out there handing out sandwiches and eats, you know. If it wasn't for them, there wouldn't be much eating.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: But, it was quite an experience of going into the service now and seeing what it was like.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that tough when you first went in thrown in with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, it was different. But, of course, the first thing you had to do was make a bunk, bunk up, so, you asked a guy how he was doing it. And you say, "When did you come in? Oh, yesterday." He was an expert already. Then, you get up early in the morning and this was in Columbus. You get up early in the morning and you wait for roll call and see if your name was called and see what camp you was going to go to and you was on KP there, and either you -- my first KP was breaking eggs for French toast.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And they came across a bad egg, and I tried to throw it out, and the old Mess Sergeant says, "Throw it in. Everything goes in there." And I ran a potato peeler one time, and it was like a washing machine, and got heck for having too many peelings on the potatoes. But, it was interesting to see, you know, you ate everything, nothing went.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And I guess that's the reason most GI's weren't picky what they ate, like the kids are today.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Because you have to eat and that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during World War II, does one particularly vivid memory come to mind?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, there are a lot of things that re-lives you. Strange -- I mean, there is a lot of experiences that I didn't cover. I mean, it was just so many experiences.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes. Any other things you want to mention here for the tape, though?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Well, I think that's about as far as I want to go. I mean --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's all right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: -- as far as World War II.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: I have other theories.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're getting political.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, so, what was your reunion with your family like when you finally did get to see them?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: The first time I seen them was up in New York at -- Well, another trip, that was the time. We toured Ellis Island. We had a boat trip down there. And the Memorial Service at Ellis Island, I met these fellows, because we have a group here in this area, an association, they have been going together since the beginning after the war. So they traveled to these places. And this fellow went to the reunion and we went up there, and we were standing and I was looking for guys from Company

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: This guy hollered at me. He says, "Hey, there's two guys right behind you that's from Company A." And here these two guys were on the patrols and things that I was on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: And it was something to see them, because the last time I seen this one fellow, it was in Herkin Forest. I was hollering at him to get his head down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he?

sp.speaker: Charles Jordan, Jr.
sp.p: Yeah. But, when a person is right beside you, and then, the next thing he isn't, that's close. You have chills coming all over, and hitting so close to you, they could have blowed you to pieces. They never went off. Other times you can look for your buddies and he's cut up in a tree. I guess that's it. MR. SWOPE: Thank you.
